#10448. ‘Sex sells, fellas’: President Trump defends Jensen Huang, says he pushed for him to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO

President Donald Trump says he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate company president and CEO Jensen Huang.

On Monday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang would resume his position just 11 days after the tech mogul’s resignation. “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement on the latest development. 

The decision comes as multiple investigations—including those from the Justice Department and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission—are still ongoing. And just last week, Nvidia chairman Harvey ​Jones had said that the company would not rehire Huang, given that his conduct did not meet the company’s code of conduct. Huang had stepped down as CEO after allegedly having an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as an additional affair with a subordinate.

But after Monday’s stunning decision to reinstate Huang, Trump seemingly took some credit for the move, telling the media that he advocated for the briefly jobless boss to come back into power. 

Trump told CNBC that Huang “did nothing wrong,” and said that he spoke to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” ahead of the move, making clear that he argued on behalf of the CEO.

The president also made clear that he told the company that Huang returning to his role was the best decision in terms of national security, and for winning the AI race with adversaries like China. 

“They did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” Trump told the outlet. He added: “People say, ‘Is it a threat to have him?’ No, it’s a threat to lose him.”

When asked about Huang’s extramarital activity, Trump even went so far as to say the ordeal would help, rather than hurt, the CEO’s success. 

“I think he’s going to start off at an almost higher level,” the president said. “He’s apologized for the indiscretions, which was unfortunate. Probably, that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas.” With this remark, Trump seemed to imply that the nature of the news story being tied to affairs is what brought it so much attention.

The president seemed to double down on the sentiment on Truth Social by posting an image of Huang waving a Photoshopped red bra in the air, referencing a famous photo from the 2024 assassination attempt on Trump’s life in Pennsylvania.

Trump may have been the most influential voice, but he wasn’t the only powerful person standing behind Huang. 

An open letter to Nvidia’s board titled “Stand With Jensen” had gained more than 206,000 signatures as of Monday morning. One of them was from Elon Musk, who took to X to share that he had signed it on November 13. “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I’m signing it too,” the Tesla and SpaceX CEO wrote. 

More than 10,000 of the signers said they were current Nvidia employees, while more than 108,000 said they were shareholders. Still, while the White House and tech moguls may be behind the decision, Huang’s critics aren’t staying quiet. 

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X that Trump is “putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security.” Some Republicans even came out against Huang’s reinstatement, including Sen. John Cornyn of Texas. In response to Trump’s denial that the affair posed any risks, the outgoing GOP senator posted on X: “No national security risk? Based on what?”

However, in the wake of his reinstatement, experts are now saying it was almost inevitable, given just how irreplaceable the CEO seemed to be. 

“There were definitely a lot of people who wanted him back. The extent that the administration intervened, the extent that shareholders intervened—it ​will be impossible to know,” said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, per Reuters.

Sosnick added: “But it tells us to some extent that Jensen Huang was too big to be fired.”

Nvidia’s stocks were up 30% in the hours after Monday’s major announcement.

#10445. Memory chip and neocloud stocks soar by double digits as investors decide they love the AI trade again

In a stunning turnaround, Nvidia’s board reinstated ousted founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, president, and as a member of the board, effective immediately on Monday, sending Nvidia’s (Nasdaq: NVDA) stock soaring over 30% along with a host of memory chip stocks.

Given Nvidia’s position as a leader in artificial intelligence, the news had a ripple effect in the infrastructure and networking AI space.

Shares of a number of memory and storage stocks were up double digits on Monday morning as of this writing:

  • Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU) up over 19%
  • Sandisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK) up 16%
  • Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC) up 14%
  • Seagate Technology Holdings (Nasdaq: STX) up 14%

Neoclouds float back to the sky

And that’s not all. Shares of neocloud providers CoreWeave, Inc. (Nasdaq: NCRWV) rose over 22%, while shares Nebius Group N.V. (Nasdaq: NBIS) jumped 24%.

To be fair, technology stocks were already rebounding before news hit on Monday—after last week’s sharp sell-off, which saw all three major market averages end in a correction by Friday.

By Monday morning, many investors apparently saw an opportunity to buy low.  

The S&P 500 (^GSPC) was up 5% after seven brutal days of declines, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose 3%, and the Nasdaq (^IXIC) was up 6.8%, at the time of this writing Monday afternoon, according to Yahoo Finance.

“The market’s explosive reaction reflects just how critical Huang is to investor confidence, and I believe his reinstatement could serve as a catalyst for a much broader recovery in AI related stocks,” David Miller, CIO and senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds, tells Fast Company. “While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today’s announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector.”

The reversal—both in the market gains and Jensen Huang’s luck—is just the latest chapter in the Nvidia cofounder’s ongoing drama that reads straight out of a spy thriller.

The saga is complete with not one, not two, but three alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman feared to be working for Chinese intelligence. It comes less than two weeks after Huang’s resignation, and after President Donald Trump said on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia’s board about reinstating Huang.

“I believe my intervention was very important . . . I convinced them . . . I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC Monday morning, adding Huang “did nothing wrong.”

#10441. Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

The Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather. Yet for almost two centuries, a central question about them remained unsolved. We knew the equations worked in practice, but no one had proven whether they always hold up mathematically without breaking down.

That all changed in September when OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem, followed on October 6 by a torrent of proposed breakthroughs across nearly 400 math problems that had baffled researchers for generations. As Cornell University mathematician Steven Strogatz explained in an Atlantic essay, the announcements have left the field reeling. How should people think about their work when a machine can do it so much better?

Strogatz is no ordinary mathematician. A pioneer in the field of nonlinear systems and network science, he is also an award-winning author and a sometime New York Times columnist. His livelihood is not in danger. Yet OpenAI has him asking, “What’s the point?” It’s a question we’re all going to have to answer. Here are three principles that will help you figure it out. 


Principle 1: The Infinite Monkey Theorem

The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges had a fascination with a concept known as the infinite monkey theorem. The idea is that if you had an infinite number of monkeys pecking away at an infinite number of typewriters, they would randomly create the collected works of Tolstoy and every other masterwork ever written (or that could be written).

Clearly, today we are living in our own version of the infinite monkey theorem, which is what Strogatz was getting at in his Atlantic piece. If you can have infinite agents attacking every aspect of an age-old problem, solving it over a period of hours, what is the value of a mathematician’s work? Is it even worth pursuing? 

Borges, in his story The Library of Babel, gave us—and mathematicians like Strogatz—some guidance about creating value in a world of infinite monkeys. First, there is the problem of curation. Yes, infinite monkeys could write War and Peace, but good luck finding it amongst all the flotsam and jetsam. We’re seeing the problem in real life today. While AI should theoretically be ramping up productivity, in reality, workers are drowning in workslop. 

The second problem is that of intent. War and Peace isn’t just meaningful for the words it contains, but because of what Leo Tolstoy intended when he wrote them. In much the same way, while it is true that artificial intelligence can run circles around human mathematicians, it is also true that humans chose the problems that OpenAI solved, and they chose them because humans found them meaningful and, possibly, useful. 

So one way that mathematicians—or anyone else—can find meaning and value in the age of AI is by acting as curators and as principal agents. Humans can choose the work that gets done according to what is meaningful to them and other humans. You could see the seeds of that idea in Strogatz’s piece. Even if all problems are solvable, we still need to choose which ones we want to solve. 

Principle 2: The economics of automation

Another way to think about how you find meaning and create value in the age of AI is to analyze the economics of automation. One effective framework involves examining three constituent forces: the displacement effect, the productivity effect, and the reinstatement effect. Together, they can help us determine where threats and opportunities might lie.

The displacement effect refers to jobs that are replaced by an automating technology—in this case, AI. The productivity effect refers to the increase in output per given unit of input due to the technological advance. The reinstatement effect refers to new jobs made possible by a technological advance.

To understand how the three effects work together, it’s helpful to look at the life of Henry Ford. Growing up on a family farm, young Henry would once have been expected to remain in the fields. But as agricultural productivity increased, he had more opportunities beyond the farm. He eventually went to work for Thomas Edison and later created an entirely new automobile industry, reinstating millions of jobs both directly and indirectly.

In the case of Henry Ford, the story was a happy one. The productivity and reinstatement effects dwarfed the displacement effect and everybody, for the most part, was better off. But the AI data is fuzzy. We are certainly seeing early signs of the displacement effect as people lose jobs, but so far we’ve seen few signs of a significant productivity or reinstatement effect. 

Still, understanding the economics of automation can help us find value and meaning. Clearly, with answers to tough problems so much more accessible, mathematicians—and other experts—can help the rest of us formulate good problems to apply to real-world challenges. Some value will likely shift from solving problems to finding good questions. 

3. Jevons Paradox and the O-Ring model

During the Industrial Revolution—which the AI age is often compared to—James Watt’s steam engine used coal much more efficiently than Thomas Newcomen’s version. So, many assumed that coal use would go down. But English economist William Stanley Jevons saw that just the opposite was happening. Coal use was actually increasing. 

Ever since, that phenomenon has been known as the Jevons paradox, the effect that occurs when technological improvements that increase the efficiency of a resource’s use lead to a rise, rather than a fall, in its use. If price elasticity is high enough, the decrease in costs encourages people to find more uses for that resource and demand increases. 

Another useful concept is the O-ring theory of economic development, which gets its name from the Challenger space shuttle disaster. The shuttle, for the most part, was in good working order, but a malfunction in an O-ring seal due to unusually cold weather led to a massive midair explosion. The point is that every job is made up of many interdependent tasks, and if even a single one fails, the entire thing doesn’t work. 

We’re seeing signs of both effects in the AI economy. While software developers can outsource many coding tasks to AI, they still need humans for others, such as communicating and collaborating with other experts on the team. Nevertheless, with code being produced so much more efficiently, job postings for software developers are on the rise. 

Strogatz may find something similar happening in mathematics. After all, there are many facets of his job that don’t involve developing proofs. He is a teacher, a writer, and an incredible translator of complex mathematical concepts for laypeople. Maybe more mathematicians can follow suit,  helping experts in other fields solve important problems with mathematical insights. 

The future of technology is always more human

Technological revolutions are always fraught, with plenty of optimism, anxiety, and visions of doom to go around. A breakthrough proves to be transformational, attracting investment that overestimates the opportunity. Boom leads to bust. Jobs are displaced, then new ones appear and, at some point, we look back and it all seems as if it were preordained. 

Yet when you’re in the midst of disruption, there is little comfort. Yes, things tend to work out in the aggregate, but many are often left worse off. In fact, despite all of the incredible technological advances of the last half-century, a 2018 Pew Research study found that Americans’ real incomes have remained essentially unchanged, with many households far worse off. 

Today, there is no shortage of opinions about where AI is taking us. Tech entrepreneurs claim that we are on the brink of such a productivity boom that it will lead to a new age of abundance—if, of course, it doesn’t kill us. Economists are much more muted, seeing meager gains amid massive overinvestment. Yet for most of us, those macro-trends aren’t nearly as important as how AI will affect us—and our well-being—directly.

The good news is that we have good tools to help us navigate our way through. The infinite monkey theorem highlights the importance of curation and intent. The economics of automation reveals the need for productivity growth to finance reinstatement. The Jevons paradox and the O-ring model encourage us to identify our place within increasingly complex ecosystems. 

AI can give us answers, but it can’t tell us what questions we want to ask. In the future, that’s where human value and meaning will increasingly lie.

#10439. Automating Contract Signing in Node.js: Webhooks, Verification, and Storing Signed PDFs

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

#10436. Thanksgiving travelers brace for airline system failures and storms

Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares.

No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.

On top of all that, there’s concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Flight delays and cancellations

The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.

First there was the Federal Aviation Administration’s network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.

Delta said Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.

“Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline said.

As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed.

Round-trip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper.

Wicked weather on both coasts

Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s midsection, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day, and reach Maine by Friday, he said.

The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).

The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue.

“This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.”

Rainy and windy weather was also expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

Thanksgiving snow for some in the U.S.

Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning, with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said.

Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state, and northwestern Pennsylvania.

“Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.”

—By John Seewer, Associated Press

Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack and Dave Collins contributed to this story.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An inspired developer has shoehorned a language model onto a floppy disk created especially for 486DX and Pentium PC users running DOS. Please note that WollyMonjac’s project isn’t a large language model (LLM). Though it shares the transformer model architecture of its much bigger siblings, Tiny 2.1 is humbly described as “a tiny question-answering transformer written in Turbo C 2.0.”

There isn’t much room for modern software on a floppy disk, with a typical PC formatted disk in the 486 era boasting just shy of 1,475,000 bytes of data capacity. Tiny 2.1 makes the best use of this limited headroom as possible, fitting in the following:

Your creaky old PC will need about 540KB of free conventional memory to run Tiny 2.1. If you do test it, we are sure you will appreciate the clean UI with its conversation history pane, neural monitor panel, and Ask Tiny prompt window. As all DOS programs should, there’s a range of F-key shortcuts highlighted within the UI. Perhaps the retro-futuristic cherry on the cake, though, is the PC-speaker robot voice which can be used to speak the responses.

We’ve already indicated that the dev seems rather humble about this DOS program. The GitHub repository says it was “Written by Fable 5.2 and trained by Opus 5.5.” Monjac also wryly admits that outside of this language model’s training, “it makes things up confidently.” We have heard less about LLM hallucinations in recent months, but here it feels almost like a fun feature.

Should any of Tiny 2.1’s knowledge gaps irk you, WollyMonjac has included a training folder in the MIT-licensed distribution. A dedicated user could probably build up a capable question-answer transformer tailored to their favorite topic(s).

Nowadays it is pretty easy to get old software to run on your shiny new hardware, one way or another. It isn’t entirely a one-way street, though; getting modern apps or games to run on hardware from decades earlier is an exciting development trend we are seeing established. In addition to the headlining Tiny 2.1, we’ve reported on similarly incongruous new-meets-old software projects like the ChatGPT client for DOS, or Minecraft running on a Game Boy, creating images on the C64 with generative AI, or playing Doom on an Atari ST.

#10433. How fast-food workers are being ranked and reprimanded with AI

Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see.

The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting-edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. Each trip is scored from 0 to 100 based on factors including acceleration, braking, cornering, and speed. According to Kearney, drivers at their store are expected to keep their scores above 85. Anyone below that score is written up by managers and eventually locked out of the Domino’s system. “Drivosity can effectively fire people,” Kearney said.

As a driver captain, Kearney has to write up other drivers, even though they have found the app doesn’t recognize the nuance of many real-world situations. Drivers can be penalized for sudden braking to avoid a collision or rapid acceleration to merge on a highway, forcing them to choose between risking an accident or getting points docked, according to Kearney. “It’s infuriating,” Kearney said. “The AI can tell you you haven’t driven well enough and you get fired.” 

Drivosity also sells coaching and analytics features, including HustleTime, which measures how fast employees walk from the store to their car, how long they take handing the pizza to a customer, and how long they take walking back. In Drivosity’s promotional videos, franchise owners and managers at Domino’s and Papa John’s praise HustleTime’s ability to track workers in real time, down to the second. Stores can “gamify” this, according to the company website, by having workers compete for better scores. 

Domino’s and Drivosity did not respond to requests for comment. 

Fast-food companies are increasingly using AI-powered technology to turn worker behavior—how fast you drive, how warmly you greet a customer, how long you spend in the bathroom—into data that can score, rank, discipline, and manage employees. To understand how these AI-driven tools are impacting fast-food workers, Capital & Main interviewed over a dozen workers, researchers, and labor advocates, who described error-prone technologies being deployed at a rapid pace, without the consent or awareness of staff, even as their pay and promotions are increasingly shaped by AI-enabled monitoring. 

“They basically use their population of workers as guinea pigs,” Alexandra Mateescu, a researcher at the nonprofit Data & Society, said of the way that fast-food companies are deploying these new tools.

* * *

In February, Burger King announced that an OpenAI-powered assistant named Patty was being rolled out at about 500 U.S. restaurants, with plans to reach all U.S. stores by the end of 2026. A few weeks later, the tool arrived at the Burger King in Niagara Falls, New York, where Dante Vasquez took drive-thru orders. 

“It started with a little AI voice in our headset,” said Vasquez.

Then the monitoring features started. Each drive-thru conversation was scored on friendliness and upselling, with the numbers displayed on a screen in front of Vasquez as he worked. Anyone could click on a transaction to hear a recording and review the AI-generated transcripts. Green boxes marked what he’d done well — a “Good morning!” or “You rule!” Red boxes marked what Patty counted against him: points off for saying “please hold,” or “um,” or not speaking clearly. 

Managers watched the scores closely, constantly reminding the crew to stay above the 70% friendliness target, Vasquez said. Workers who scored low were cut from the schedule, he added. 

Vasquez learned to speak the way that Patty wanted. He got so good at it that customers started asking if he was a bot. His co-workers nicknamed him “Gemini” [Google’s AI assistant].

“The system wants me to talk like a robot, so I’m talking like a robot,” Vasquez said. “It just gets so mentally degrading.”

Burger King has said publicly that the system was not designed to evaluate individual employees. But Capital & Main reviewed screenshots from a Burger King training module, and images of the dashboard in use, showing individual drive-thru conversations time-stamped and marked for tone and upselling. Vasquez, and other Burger King employees, some of whom spoke to Capital & Main on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said it was easy to identify and discipline individual employees for low scores. 

Later, Patty started scoring workers on “warmth,” a metric Vasquez couldn’t make sense of. When he asked his district manager how it was calculated, he recalled, she told him to just talk “like a warm blanket.” 

According to Vasquez, Patty seemed to penalize his Black co-workers more than others for what the system flagged as “improper tone.” Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said that scoring workers on warmth or friendliness is “sort of pseudoscience” and that those tools risk penalizing workers for their accents or disabilities. 

Asked to respond to these concerns, Kristen Viersen, Burger King’s director of communications, emailed Capital & Main a company statement that said, “We have never before heard any example similar to the questions you raised about team members being penalized based on race, gender, ethnicity, or accent.” Burger King declined to answer when asked if the company had tested these features for bias. 

The new monitoring features were intended “to celebrate great examples of friendly service” and allow managers to coach their team, according to the statement, which also said that Burger King has since disabled both features “for further improvements.” Burger King would not say when the features were disabled, and workers said the monitoring was active through August of this year.

Co-workers at Vasquez’s restaurant joked that Vasquez would soon be gone, replaced by Patty entirely, a looming threat that was amplified by a sign in the store that reminded workers that Patty was being trained on every headset conversation. Eventually, the stress just wasn’t worth it. 

He quit in August.

 “If Patty wasn’t introduced,” Vasquez said, “I would still be working at Burger King.”

* * *

While large chains have struck high-profile deals with major AI companies—Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC, and Habit Burger & Grill, announced last year that it was deploying Nvidia-powered computer vision for “back-of-house labor management through real-time analytics and alerts”—a crowd of smaller vendors sells the same kind of AI monitoring to individual franchisees, with far less visibility.

Among the more established vendors is Solink, an Ottawa-based company backed by Goldman Sachs that describes itself as “the leader in AI-driven video intelligence.” It works with franchisees of Domino’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, Jack in the Box, Five Guys, and other chains. 

Solink’s product documentation describes a video-surveillance system capable of flagging workers who arrive late or leave early, take too long on their breaks, fail to wear a hairnet or the correct uniform, use their phones while on the clock, or simply stand idle. The software can layer onto a restaurant’s existing security cameras, and it lets managers type in prompts to find footage of specific behaviors or set up automatic alerts.

In a statement, a Solink spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company’s platform helps businesses “improve operations, sales, safety, and customer experience.” It also stressed that Solink “does not offer identification tools such as biometrics or facial recognition,” and that its terms require customers to comply with the law.

Data & Society’s Mateescu said these tools are rarely marketed as worker surveillance. Instead they are sold as “loss prevention” or “workflow management” tools. This language, she said, obscures what the technology actually does “both to employees and to consumers.”

* * *

While some companies use corporate euphemisms to obscure worker monitoring, others are more direct. MashMore, a new potato-themed fast-food restaurant in Albany, New York, is explicit about its AI use. Using commercially available AI models, its co-founders built an HR chatbot, named Mashy after the store’s mascot, that schedules, scores, and ranks all employees.

Mashy runs on a stream of data employees generate as they work. Workers clock into routines, complete assigned “quests,” and upload photos proving that tasks are completed. In exchange, they earn “Mashy points,” which set their level in the restaurant’s ranking system and can determine bonuses and promotions.

When co-founder and CEO Andy Gor let Capital & Main interact with the chatbot, it didn’t hesitate about who the employee of the month should be. “Shontia Thomas, and it genuinely isn’t a contest,” the chatbot wrote on a screen that Gor shared with a reporter. Gor said the system would never be used to fire an employee, but the chatbot had created rankings for all workers, including those with the lowest scores. 

Gor wants to make every routine, cleaning task and customer-service expectation tracked, scored, and eventually copied from one location to another, so he can check anything from anywhere. “I’m in China right now,” he said. “I can see that during rush hour they cleaned the table nicely. Today, they pass.”

MashMore currently has just one location, but Gor wants to franchise fast. His pitch to investors is that the AI tool can manage employees across dozens of locations. Mashy, Gor said, is “our boss. Basically I’m working for him, too.”

* * *

Efforts to rein in algorithmic management have mostly stalled at the federal level. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of first-in-the-nation workplace-AI laws on September 30. SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act, bars employers from relying solely on AI to fire or discipline workers. AB 1883 prohibits tools that use AI to infer an employee’s emotional state or collect “neural data.” SB 951 requires employers to notify workers when AI is behind a mass layoff.

Tobin-Miyaji said in an email that the emotion-scoring ban would likely cover a tool like Patty—but that No Robo Bosses could be satisfied by “cursory” human oversight, leaving workers “constantly surveilled and quantified.” 

Unions could in theory negotiate stricter protections than legislation might afford. In 2023, workers in California won the creation of a Fast Food Council, a state body empowered by law to set wages and weigh in on working conditions across the industry. But despite worker efforts to apply pressure to Gov. Newsom, the council currently lacks a chairperson and has not met for over a year. A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.”

Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off. 

When Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he said they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t plan to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing.

Ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.”

—By Z Waite

This piece was originally published by Capital & Main.

#10432. AI features could be turned off with a simple toggle, Canva proves

AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available. If you’ve ever wanted to just turn off AI features, Canva proves that it could be a simple toggle, if companies actually wanted to give you a choice.

Canva today announced “AI Controls,” a new toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.

Generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference. Canva puts this well:

For some people, AI is the most exciting creative tool in a generation, while others prefer bringing their ideas to life without it. We believe the future of creativity should give everyone the freedom to choose their own path, whether that’s creating with AI, without it, or somewhere in between.

To give its users the choice, Canva’s Permissions menu now has a simple toggle for “Enable Generative AI features.” Toggling it off disables features such as Magic Write and Magic Edit. There’s also an option to limit how much AI-generated imagery appears in the Canva library.

AI has its place, but everyone should have a choice like this, especially when it comes to apps and services used for artistry in the same vein as Canva. Yet, the tech industry continues to go in the opposite direction, shoving AI into every corner whether it’s actually useful or not. Canva proves, though, that it doesn’t have to be that way.

Hopping around the electricity grid, recharging on power lines, NOMADs don’t need to come home.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tech startup Nomadic showcased its NOMAD drones this week alongside an announcement that it had raised $6 million in seed funding. These quadcopter drones have a unique skill hinted at by their name: they can basically fly forever without returning to base. NOMADs recharge by perching on high-voltage power lines, a ubiquitous feature of most landscapes, before moving on to their next task.

We hadn’t heard anything about the NOMAD drones until now, but Nomadic says it has tested its quadcopters for over 20,000 hours on live lines in Germany, Norway, and the U.S. “NOMADs are drones that land on live high-voltage lines, charge from the line itself, and relocate across the grid to where measurements are needed,” summarizes the startup.

The reference to measurements along the power grid reveals the current purpose of NOMAD drones. They are deployed to monitor the high-voltage lines from which they leech their energy. This is a very useful task for power companies. Nomadic explains that while modern grid operators use weather models to decide how much power each line can carry, the qualities of the lines can be quite variable. Meanwhile, the weakest point in any line “sets the limit for the whole line,” says the startup.

Fixed sensors have started to become the accepted solution for line monitoring, but mobile drones are a tantalizing alternative. In comparison to fixed sensors, the NOMAD, which recharges inductively from the line itself, seems like an ideal solution. Normally, an investigative high-voltage power line check with a human operator would also require extensive planning, heavy machinery, and the line to lose power for a short service period. Nomadic claims that a NOMAD drone can look after around 25km of line, while fixed sensors are typically positioned from 1km to 5km apart.

In addition to the drone hardware, there’s some integrated software to make the best use of the highly configurable data you can harvest from your drone fleet. “Nomadic OS combines their data with weather and grid models, giving operators a real-time picture of what is physically happening on their lines.”

NOMAD drones are also surprisingly tough. Units have been tested in temperatures as low as minus 25 degrees Celsius, in strong winds, and on lines up to 420kV (European transmission grid typical maximum). With the new funding, Nomadic is hoping to expand its fleet and build with more partners. The startup is also looking for several new recruits, mostly in engineering roles, all based in Munich, Germany.

#10429. Abdul El-Sayed rebranded ‘Medicare For All’ to get Trump’s attention. It worked

Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan campaigned on passing Medicare For All, a universal single-payer national health insurance system. He believes in the initiative so much, he’s even willing to rebrand it to an unlikely name.

In mid-November, El Sayed posted an image on social media of a gold card emblazoned with name “TrumpCare.” The mockup was a convincing depiction of what a TrumpCare insurance card might look like. Trump’s name and signature is in the bottom right-hand corner, and there’s a presidential-style seal on it as well as the tagline “Great Health Care For Every American.”

“Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote on X on November 12.

The card was designed to get President Donald Trump’s attention—and it did. On Saturday, Trump reshared a screenshot of the card on his social network without comment on Saturday. Vice President JD Vance’s office reached out to El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting NBC News reported Sunday.

Republicans and others learned long ago that the key to Trump’s attention and heart is flattery, especially when it comes to design and branding. There’s already Trump passports, the “Trump Gold Card,” for visas, and “TrumpRx,” a prescription drug website. A proposal for children’s investment accounts previously called “Money Accounts for Growth and Advancement” for “MAGA” were renamed simply as “Trump Accounts” to be included in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Architectural firms that submitted a proposal to Trump’s Department of Transportation for a new terminal at Dulles Airport just outside Washington, D.C., slapped Trump’s name on it in their renderings.

El-Sayed’s proposal to turn Medicare For All policy into pictures that Trump understands, is part of larger democratic playbook. Recall when New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani showed up to the Oval Office with an imagined New York Daily News front page with the headline “Trump to City: Let’s Build” to encourage Trump to support federal grants for housing construction in the city.

El-Sayed’s rebranded proposal shows that Democrats have now picked up on how to win over Trump’s favor when it comes to passing your agenda. Meet Trump where he’s at. In an Instagram video, El-Sayed appeals to Trump’s low approval ratings and pitching passing “TrumpCare” as a chance to redeem himself, and on Meet the Press Sunday, he called it “the ultimate Trump card.”

Medicare For All is popular, but winning over Trump and Republicans could be key to actually getting a proposal passed. An October KFF poll found 66% of U.S. adults “strongly” or “somewhat support” a national health plan, but it’s far more popular among Democrats (84%) and independents (72%) than it is among Republicans (34%). Trump has previously said Medicare For All “doesn’t work” and called it “a socialist takeover of our healthcare system.”

Though Democrats will have control of the next Congress beginning in January, Trump will still have the power of the veto to block legislation. To override that veto, Democrats will need Republican support to reach a total of 290 votes in the House and 67 votes in the Senate. Or they could avoid a veto altogether by getting Trump on board. A shiny gold card could be all it takes.

#10428. Preventing API Contract Drift in TypeScript Applications

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a new optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A typical configuration might look like this:

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

These tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

#10426. Proton Pass is up to 60% off for Black Friday—and it does way more than just store your passwords

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Proton Pass is designed to take that friction out of your day. It creates strong, unique passwords, remembers them for you, and fills them in when you log in. But it also handles something a password alone can’t: keeping your real email address out of another retailer’s database.

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

Proton Pass does that work for you. When you sign up for a website, its password generator can create a strong password that’s completely unique. Save it in your vault, and Proton Pass can fill in your credentials when you return.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new users and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

#10425. Making six figures? You might still be using buy now, pay later, according to new research

We are a nation united in our desire to pay tomorrow for what we’re buying today.

In the past decade, various deferred payment options have grown in popularity and new data from Block might buck the notion of who the “typical” customer is. Once favored by younger shoppers and those consumers who had limited access to credit, households earning more than $100,000 per year are actually more likely to opt for some of these deferred payment options now, according to the Oakland, California-based fintech company.

Buy now, pay later (BNPL) or checkout financing is the most popular among the 66% of American adults between the ages of 18 and 59 surveyed by Block who have used a deferred-payment option in the past year. And honing in on those households earning more than $100,000 per year, 69% had used BNPL or checkout financing in the past 12 months compared with 65% of households earning between $50,000 and $100,000 and 61% of those earning less than $50,000, the study found.

But it’s not just BNPL that’s increasingly popular among the highest earning Americans. Block’s study found that four of seven different deferred-payment options were more commonly used by the highest earners, including the option to split a purchase into payments after making it or using an installment plan from a store, provider or lender.

Though Block has a dog in the race—it owns Afterpay and Cash App, both of which offer deferred-payment options—the company contends that their growing popularity isn’t necessarily a sign that people are spending beyond their means. Rather, the company found that 72% of users financed at least one expense in the past year that they technically had the money for, but paying upfront would have felt like a strain, while 47% opted to spread out payments to leave money set aside for savings, investments or other priorities.

The report shows how people weigh the tradeoffs of the cost of financing versus keeping cash in their accounts. 

“People don’t look at their checking balance and think of it all as money they ⁠can spend,” Juan Hernandez, head of credit and underwriting at Block told Reuters. “​Some of it is already set aside ​for rent, some is for the next bill, and some they want to keep in case something ​goes wrong.”

FINANCING SHOWS STRAIN

Even so, some of the Block data underscores the strain that many Americans are feeling amid the current affordability crisis that’s seen people struggle to pay for everyday expenses. That’s important as consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of gross domestic product and while Americans have largely weathered the current affordability crisis, one measure of consumer confidence recently fell to the lowest level since 2014. 

The Block study found that people are using deferred-payment methods to finance everyday purchases, like groceries, filling up their tank at the gas station or to pay their utility bills. To cover groceries and other bills, cash advances, earned wage access and/or short-term loans accounted for 58% of these financed transactions. 

And even though a vast majority of consumers—82% of those financing basics and 73% who are financing bills—reported repayment horizons for these expenses within six weeks, that still shows that many people are struggling to keep pace with their day-to-day expenses.

Such data underscores the findings of a recent survey by Pew Research Center. Among American adults surveyed in August, 27% said they can’t pay some of their monthly bills—or can only afford to make partial payments.

The so-called blue tsunami that saw Democrats take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections also gave these politicians a mandate to address affordability. And Hakeem Jeffries, the current Speaker-Designate of the House, indicated last week that will be among the priorities for the new Congress come January.

“We’re going to relentlessly fight for an affordable America,” Jeffries said in a press conference. “We’re going to work hard to drive down the high cost of groceries and gas and housing.”

Creditors want to ensure they could still sell the AI chips in case SpaceX defaults on its loan.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk is borrowing $43 billion to finance SpaceX's acquisition of Nvidia AI chips for its ambitious data center projects and is using the semiconductors as collateral. However, Ars Technica reports that lenders are concerned that SpaceX will use the chips for its planned orbital data center, making it difficult, if not impossible, for creditors to reclaim in case the company defaults on its loan. SpaceX said it will deploy the collateralized chips only on Earth, but it remains unclear whether this provision is included in the signed debt instrument.

SpaceX is working on building massive data centers on both Earth and in space. Musk has already revealed the company’s first-generation AI1 satellite, with a 120-kilowatt payload and a span that’s larger than a Boeing 747, while he’s also planning to build a $24-billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Starbase, Texas. These projects are in addition to the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 sites near the Tennessee-Mississippi border.

Despite being one of the richest people on Earth right now, Musk is relying on a financing deal to acquire the chips he needs to achieve his dream of building an AI LLM that will “assist in the pursuit of understanding.” The $43 billion “Project Saturn” loan is also not structured like a typical loan, so its investment-grade rating would remain unaffected. Instead, it’s built similarly to aircraft leasing agreements, in which a leasing company buys the jets and leases them to the airline that wants to use them. This saves the airline from having to put up a significant amount of cash to get the airplanes that it needs.

For this deal, the Saturn Funding Trust, a fully owned subsidiary of asset-backed lending company WHCO, would acquire the Nvidia GPUs for SpaceX, with the latter paying the former quarterly for the privilege of using the AI chips. The deal is also described as a “five-year triple-net, hell-or-high-water finance lease arrangement,” meaning SpaceX must pay the lease for five years, whether the chips break, become obsolete, or the project becomes unprofitable. It’s also responsible for all the expenses of operating the chips.

These terms are very lender-friendly, as SpaceX basically assumes all the risks while also keeping them off its books. Rating agency Moody’s also said in its report that the chips will be deployed in SpaceX’s U.S. data centers. Nevertheless, the company’s plan to blast data centers into space is making some lenders nervous, regardless of its Earth-bound plans and promises.

#10421. Spotify Wrapped 2026 is almost here. Here’s how to make sure you’re ready

Its that time of year again: when people flood social media with year-end reviews and music lovers start counting down to what may be the most anticipated of them all: Spotify Wrapped.

Spotify Wrapped 2026 reveals not just your top five songs, those embarrassing tunes on repeat, it stacks your minutes and musical tastes up against the general public—for better or for worse. (In past years, it also revealed listeners most-streamed songs, favorite artists, and podcasts.)

Last year, some 500 million users shared their stories all over social media in the first 24 hours, an overall increase of 41% year-over-year (YOY) from the year before.

When Does Spotify Wrapped drop?

While the company hasn’t officially announced the release date for Spotify Wrapped 2026, the streaming platform’s past history reveals some good clues about when to expect it—and that date is coming up fast.

Last year, Spotify Wrapped dropped soon after Thanksgiving on December 3. The previous year, in 2024, it came out one day later on December 4 and before that, in 2023 and 2022, it came out November 29, and 30, respectfully, near Thanksgiving weekend.

However, since 2021, Spotify Wrapped has released on a Wednesday, often right after Thanksgiving, which falls on December 2, 2026 this year.

A look at online prediction market Kalshi shows traders give Spotify Wrapped 2026 only a 21% chance of it dropping before Dec 2, 2026, but forecast an 88% chance before December 3, and a 90% before Dec 4, 2026.

How can I see Spotify Wrapped once it releases?

Spotify listeners can view their personalized recap in Spotify’s mobile app and share results on social media platforms including Instagram and TikTok.

To get the updated app, scan the QR code to download Spotify.
