#10417. Everything that led to Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO

Jensen Huang is back as CEO, just 11 days after his closely watched exit from Nvidia—and even as he remains mired in controversy. 

In an announcement this morning, the Nvidia board claimed to be “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA,” following a number of meetings with the newly reinstated CEO. The chairman said the board “believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA” and that his return atop the company is “in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.” 

There was little mention of the circumstances that led to Huang’s departure, aside from an assurance that the board had conferred with senior government officials and were now “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” The announcement noted that an independent investigation was still underway—to probe the fallout from Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy—and that he intended to cooperate. 

Huang’s reinstatement is not entirely a surprise (though it was apparently a surprise to interim CEO Colette Kress, who was not consulted on the decision, per a Bloomberg report). By the board’s own admission, the decision seems to have been influenced by President Trump, who has remained a steadfast supporter of Huang throughout this entire debacle. But Trump was more explicit about his role in a CNBC interview today, where he revealed that he spoke directly to the company’s board. “And I convinced them,” he said. “I made the deal.” Trump also noted that “we have to protect our geniuses.”

As Fast Company reported earlier today, Huang’s return underscores his influence as a key player in the AI boom (not to mention his cozy relationship with Trump). Since Huang resigned, there has been a steady drumbeat of concern from the tech community, with prominent figures like Elon Musk and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick arguing that he should be reinstated. 

At the New York Times’s DealBook summit last week, Musk argued that “there’s no one that can really replace Jensen” and likened his resignation to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” (Other leaders at the conference also spoke highly of Huang, from Sam Altman to Anduril’s Palmer Luckey.) In a recent appearance, Kalanick drew parallels to his own experience being ousted from Uber and said “we gotta bring Jensen back.” Y Combinator cofounder Paul Graham boldly asserted that “I’ve never known the tech world to be more unanimous about anything than they are about Jensen Huang.”

Despite allegations of multiple inappropriate relationships with his own employees—including a direct report—plenty of Nvidia employees have also expressed solidarity with Huang. 

A Wired report last week revealed that some employees immediately urged the board to bring Huang back in internal posts. A widely circulated petition to reinstate Huang as CEO drew over 200,000 signatures, of which over 10,000 were from current Nvidia employees—about a quarter of the company’s workforce. Musk, Kalanick, and a handful of other CEOs and business leaders also signed the petition.

It didn’t take long for Huang to plead his case. 

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” he said last week, hours before the company’s first earnings call without him. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” He also acknowledged that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA” and had made “serious mistakes in my personal life.” At the time, the board continued to insist that there was no plan to bring him back.

But now that Huang is at the helm again, is it back to business as usual? There are all kinds of questions about what his return could mean for Nvidia—and not just in terms of the serious national security concerns raised by his indiscretions. 

The board is still conducting an investigation into the events that led to Huang’s exit, but it could be little more than a formality if he has already been reinstated. (Or perhaps the board will find itself in yet another bind when that investigation surfaces new information.) 

While the board now claims to be convinced of Huang’s candor, it was quite the opposite just two weeks ago, per a Wired report, when his “lack of candor” and “lying” apparently pushed the board to remove him. As Fast Company previously reported, boards usually also have little tolerance for CEOs pursuing romantic relationships with their subordinates (and the stock price often takes a dip following those revelations). 

Nvidia also has an unusually flat organizational structure, in which Huang has 60 direct reports, an arrangement that seems to have left the company without much of a succession plan—while making its CEO even more powerful. 

A New York Times investigation last week raised further concerns over Huang’s leadership at Nvidia, which seems to have created a culture of fear at the company. While many employees remain loyal to Huang—and even seem to revere him—others claim to have experienced ritual humiliation under his rule. Over a dozen former and current employees said Huang frequently used insults and personal attacks to motivate his staff. 

According to the Times, Huang could be particularly creative with his insults, telling an executive that his mother should have aborted him and in another instance threatening to rip off an employee’s head and “pee on your brain.” 

The report found that Huang’s management style had sparked regular HR complaints—though some employees said they weren’t adequately addressed—and that a former HR leader had been fired for calling attention to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” that he had seen in his career. (The former employee threatened to sue but ultimately reached a settlement with Nvidia for over $1 million, the Times reported.)

At the moment, it’s not clear how or whether Nvidia plans to address these issues, along with Huang’s other transgressions. His statement today stops short of introspection or any insight into what—if anything—could change upon his return. 

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in his statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

It remains to be seen whether Huang will approach the job any differently. But in the meantime, since news of his return broke this morning, Nvidia stock is up over 30%.

#10415. At $600, the Pixel 10 is this year’s no-brainer Black Friday smartphone deal

Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a new device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list.

While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year. From a hardware perspective, nearly everything is either identical or close enough to not particularly matter. Its design and display are all but unchanged, Qi2-ready magnets come on both models, and both devices are built with the same level of battery longevity in mind. And much to the chagrin of many a Pixel die-hard, Tensor G5 and Tensor G6 are practically interchangeable.

So what are you giving up that matters? When the Pixel 11 arrived, software features made up the bulk of this list, but with last week’s Pixel Drop, a lot of the gaps between these two generations have been closed. Gemini Intelligence with Rambler, app automation, and more are in the process of rolling out to existing Pixel 10 users, and new features like Create My Widget arrived on the Pixel 10 and 11 at the exact same time. From a software perspective — Google’s bread and butter, in my eyes — the only big sacrifice comes from the year of software support that’s already complete, leaving you with just six instead of seven.

Realistically, the camera is the one place you’re likely to feel a difference. The Pixel 10 was the first non-Pro device in Google’s Tensor era to ship with a telephoto lens, but it came with some big sacrifices. The main sensor is effectively an A-series lens, and taken together, the entire package might leave something to be desired. It’s far from a bad camera though — I used it as my main shooter through most of its lifecycle — and while the Pixel 11 did get some upgrades here, I think real shutterbugs would be better off looking at Google’s Pro lineup anyway. You’ll also lose out on things like HiLight, though really, are you missing that much?

What makes this deal so good is really its place in the market, not as a direct comparison to the newer Pixel 11. For $600, Google’s competition is going to have a hard time competing with the value the Pixel 10 delivers. Hell, even Google might find it difficult to compete in the coming months; at full price, $600 is what the Pixel 10a goes for now, a decidedly less-impressive device compared to this model. No, this is a flagship smartphone through and through, and for $600, you’re effectively guaranteeing a reliable, powerful smartphone experience from now until 2032 — hopefully enough time for this whole RAM crisis to finally simmer down a bit.

#10414. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

A teaser points to a Dec. 29 reveal for a card that promises four times the S80’s 16GB of memory.

Moore Threads’ MTT S80 product manager says that the next Lushan gaming GPU will have more VRAM than any consumer graphics card currently available, VideoCardz reports. With Nvidia’s RTX 5090 already at 32GB, Lushan would need more than that. This matches the previous promise of four times the company’s MTT S80’s 16GB, putting the flagship Lushan at 64GB.

Moore Threads apparently hasn’t given up on graphics, even four years after the MTT S80’s release. The company teased the card earlier this week with a poster for MDC 2026, its developer conference, showing a graphics card under a black cloth on a mountainside, and put Lushan’s name in the title of the post. It has previously indicated that Lushan products would arrive before the end of the year.

Although nothing the product manager stated is an official statement, his words suggest that the new Lushan GPU could feature the largest memory capacity yet offered on a consumer graphics card, which certainly draws a lot of attention from gamers and local AI enthusiasts alike. As it stands, the 32GB RTX 5090 was available at $6,599 in our recent Newegg check, more than three times its MSRP, which illustrates the astronomical demand.

Not disclosed; “4x” the S80 claimed, up to 64GB by our math

$1,999 MSRP; from $6,599 at Newegg (Nov. 15)

2,999 yuan with a motherboard (about $410) at launch; 1,499 yuan (about $225) at JD.com, Nov. 21

The Lushan would be a graphics rendering chip based on the Huagang architecture, with a sibling Huashan for AI. Performance claims are lofty at 15x for AAA gaming, 50x ray tracing, 64x AI compute, and 16x geometry processing over the MTT S80, based on information from MDC 2025, last year’s edition of the conference. To get there, Lushan adds a new hardware ray-tracing engine, the UniTE rendering architecture, AI generative rendering, which MyDrivers describes as the manufacturer’s answer to Nvidia’s DLSS and AMD’s FSR for upscaling and multi-frame generation, and DirectX 12 Ultimate support.This is a mighty high goal, as the previous outing, with the S80, fell short of expectations. Released in November 2022 at 2,999 yuan (about $410), the S80 was at first sold only in a bundle with an Asus motherboard. It now costs about half that in China, despite rising GPU costs. The 16GB GDDR6, PCIe 5.0 GPU, which pulls 255W, only matched a low-end card when tested on immature drivers in early 2023; it struggled against a GT 1030.

Moore Threads said last December that it had shipped monthly driver updates since and claimed the S80 then benchmarked 3.4x higher than at launch. The new 15x target is more reasonable when put against the backdrop of just how far the S80 trailed when it landed.

If we look beyond the consumer space, there are plenty of cards that have more than 32GB, and 64GB for that matter. The Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell workstation card, for instance, has 96GB of GDDR7. It’s also possible to get RTX 4090s rebuilt with 48GB, at least in some Chinese shops, and a listing in September offered an RTX 5090 modded to 96GB. Maxsun also has the Arc Pro B60 Dual, built on Intel GPUs, with 2x 24GB on just one board. However, memory supply remains tight, with crushing memory shortages, and is projected to remain so, while GDDR7 remains quite costly.

Domestic rival Lisuan’s G100, meanwhile, is only at 12GB and 24GB for consumer and enterprise. A 64GB Lushan would leave those in the dust, which may hint that Moore Threads is targeting Western cards rather than just domestic rivals. It also raises the question of just how much memory you need for certain workloads.

The Honor Watch 6 Pro has a 5,500-nit OLED display, ceramic bezel, 18-day battery life, and costs less than it looks.

In the world of athletic smartwatches, it isn’t often that you could mistake one for a luxury watch, but Honor seems to want to flip all that on its head with the Honor Watch 6 Pro. Just take a look at this excerpt from the company’s press release:

Framing this brilliant display is a Precision Nanocrystalline Ceramic bezel crafted through a 1400°C high-temperature integrated sintering process, delivering a delicate texture and rich visual depth.

Inspired by modernist architecture, its diamond-cut octagonal rotatable crown features a dual-layer horizontal and vertical cut, complemented by a side button for intuitive navigation.

That sounds pretty wild to me, and it’s backed up by specs that sound just as legit, too. On top is a 1.5-inch LTPO Tandem AMOLED display that outputs 5,500-nit peak brightness. Underneath is a bevy of new sensors called the Intelligent Sense System, which Honor says combines “multi-wavelength monitoring, multi-optical path patrol technology, and anti-interference glass technology to reach deep skin layers.”

Runners will be pleased to know that the Honor Watch 6 Pro not only incorporates a dual-band GPS, but combines it with a “star-pointing 3-antenna design” and an AI fusion algorithm, which should deliver ultra-accurate tracking in any location and no matter how you hold your wrist. Despite its luxury looks, this one tracks over 120 sports modes, including Honor’s Professional Running Coach feature, which tracks running posture, lactate threshold, heart rate targets, and keeps you on pace with real-time voice coaching.

During sports modes like Badminton, the watch can identify more than six types of swings, and Honor says other sports modes can deliver similarly detailed statistics. The watch is 5ATM, IP68, IP69, and IP69K water-and-dust-resistant rated, plus it integrates directly with Strava so you can pull all your fitness data together.

Honor is incorporating a new wrist twist gesture system this time around, letting you use gestures to perform actions hands-free. The watch is rated at 10 days of battery life on a single charge in regular usage mode, while endurance mode will stretch that to 18 days. Pre-sales begin today, November 19, and run until December 31, when the watch is expected to launch, starting at €279/£229 for early bird pricing. After launch, the retail MSRP starts at €379/£329.

Its lead shrinks to 3.83x on the 15 workloads without AI tuning.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Architect Labs, a Palo Alto startup, said in a research blog post that its AI systems discovered, designed, and verified Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set “built from the ground up.” Across 25 workloads, a four-tile Frostbite cluster delivered 4.59 times the performance per watt of a similarly sized “silicon-proven” dual-issue, in-order CPU core. Those numbers come from a simulated 7nm design that has not yet been made in silicon, and the company says it can’t name the comparison core for legal reasons.

Conventional CPUs have hardware that “rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other.” Multicore designs also need deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols, which keep every core’s view of shared memory consistent, but scale poorly and cost area and power. Architect Labs’ alternative is what it calls “multithreading for free,” where the program itself exposes the parallel work, without threads, locks, or out-of-order hardware required for that discovery.

Frostbite’s programs are compiled to interaction nets, a model of computation from 1990 in which a program is a graph of nodes and computation happens by rewriting pairs of connected nodes, and the chip is designed around this distinct paradigm. Pairs of nodes being rewritten never overlap, so they can run in any order, or all at once, and arrive at the same result. Every value is also used exactly once, so data can stay in small local memories instead of large shared caches.

An example of the difference given by the team is a 5x5 chess-like board with five queens, placed so none can attack another. A typical program searches for solutions one board at a time. As an interaction net, the same search breaks into 3,183 small operations, and the longest chain that has to run in order is only 262 steps, so on average about 12 operations are ready to run at once at each step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get there, as the parallel work was already intrinsic.

Each of the chip’s tiles, small identical processing units linked by an on-chip network, has its own small local memory. Four tiles, plus four L3 nodes, form the cluster that’s benchmarked against the conventional core for the performance claims, but the full layout has 16 tiles. The design reached 800 MHz in early synthesis but ended up at 500 MHz in the final layout. The cluster also averaged 8.77 times the comparison core’s performance per area, and the table below shows how its performance per watt varies by workload.

Frostbite performance per watt vs. comparison core

It may come as some surprise that the AI which built Frostbite started with what the company calls “zero architectural priors,” though the team first picked the workloads it had to do well on, and this sort of blank slatism may have its advantages in avoiding bias. Instead, the agents read papers and benchmarks, built Python models, and then selected one concept for focus. The original 141-page PDF output, which contained a programming model, runtime, and high-level blocks, was deleted after the first register-transfer level (RTL) design was generated, because “many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible.”

That PDF was only ever a starting point. Once the agents picked an architecture, they moved away from English — as it can’t get every detail right or catch every mistake, according to the team — and wrote the spec in the company’s own language, called ASL. ASL translates to Lean, a proof checker, so it can be machine-checked, which the company says stops a large class of bugs and cuts down on agents gaming their objectives. From this, the agents devised Arcmodel, a software model of the whole chip written in ASL, before any circuit design existed.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Simulating the RTL is slow, so the agents tested ideas on the model instead, which ran about 200 times faster. At first, the model’s power estimates were off by up to almost 250%, but an automated loop adjusted it until it matched the circuit design within just 5%.

From there, swarms of agents proposed changes in parallel, and each one was checked against the spec, tried in the fast model, built into the circuit design, and measured for power before being kept or dropped. This led to 58 ideas tried, with 37 kept. Separately, a behavior emerged that “was never specified by any human,” in what is known as work stealing: a tile with nothing to do can pull spare work from a neighbor or, in lieu of anything to do, go idle to save power.

Share of energy (one four-tile cluster, mean of 20 workloads, excluding clock distribution)

Fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions

Clock distribution (share of total energy, left out of the rows above)

This isn’t Architect Labs’ first design, as it showed off Redwood, an AI inference accelerator for robots and drones, in August. In that case, the company says its AI generated the RTL, verification, firmware, drivers, and kernels in under two weeks from a spec written by two human architects. Redwood still runs only on an FPGA and hasn’t been made in silicon, though the company says it is working toward having it built at TSMC.

Tendrils Compute, a possible rival based in Cambridge, U.K., raised funding earlier this month for a processor it says will have “thousands of cores operating in parallel.” It is also developing Vine, the same language Frostbite’s programs are written in.

Architect Labs says more benchmarks are coming, but they’re only part of the plan. It also wants an FPGA-hosted “software playground for anybody to run a program on Frostbite” along with a “preliminary operating system.” Eventually, it plans to release Frostbite’s RTL and instruction set.

In the meantime, the company plans to cover more workloads and compare “a broader set of CPUs,” including larger Frostbite mesh configurations against multicore versions of the comparison core with large caches. It also plans to test against “larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs,” with these comparisons due in the coming months on popular CPU benchmark suites such as SPEC and PARSEC.

#10403. Top 6 AI Detector Tools in 2026: Features, Accuracy Claims and When to Trust Them

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical"

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function."""

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0})

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan")

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan")

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}")

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

Chips designers have to prove that their semiconductors do not break U.S. export control rules.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has released an interim final rule (IFR) [PDF] that will prevent Chinese AI companies from leasing data compute outside of China to access advanced U.S. chips like Nvidia Blackwell AI GPUs. However, Nikkei Asia reports that the new regulations have also affected foundries making chips for consumers and the automotive industry, as TSMC has put several shipments to both Chinese and non-Chinese chip designers on hold as it reviews their compliance with the changes to U.S.

Washington’s previous export controls only focused on high-performance AI chips like Nvidia’s Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin chips. The new rules expand it to include all chips, with front-end fabricators (chip foundries) or OSATs (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies), also known as packaging and testing companies, required to assume that semiconductors with a 16nm or 14nm node are automatically classified as export-controlled advanced computing chips. The ruling even mentioned that even if the designed chip has less than 30 billion transistors and has no HBM, it cannot be assumed that the chips aren’t built for high-performance computing.

The 16nm and 14nm nodes have been around for around 10 years now, and they could even be found inside consumer devices like smartphones and TVs, as well as in automotive applications. This new rule means that designers making chips using 16nm or newer nodes, even if they’re not specifically built for data centers, must secure documentation from an approved designer certifying the chip’s Total Processing Performance or performance density if they want to avoid additional scrutiny from the fab.

"The new rule is very strict this time, and the affecting scope is far beyond only chips for data centers but covers smartphone processors, autonomous driving and other types of chips for consumer electronics as well as others if they are using nodes that are 14nm or 16nm or more advanced tech," a source told the publication. "The move would delay shipments to many chip developers worldwide before they can clear compliance and hit many emerging startups in many Asian nations."

Aside from this, the U.S. also now requires export licenses to ship advanced AI chips to the following countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil, and Thailand. The IFR says that these countries are often used as transshipment points for chips that are being diverted to China, as evidenced by the Supermicro and Megaspeed investigations, which used one of these countries as the destination of the Nvidia servers they ordered, before sending them forward to their final destination in China.

Chip smuggling has long been a simmering issue in the United States, but it seemingly has bubbled over after the revelation of Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who’s also suspected of being instrumental in diverting $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips and passing on information to Chinese intelligence. While his alleged relationship with a direct subordinate was the apparent primary cause of his departure from Nvidia, sources say that the real reason behind his ousting is the mass smuggling of 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs that happened right under his nose.

The U.S. delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions. These hand-launched uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are equipped with optical and infrared sensors for surveying the battlefield, but the evolving electromagnetic warfare landscape meant that the entire fleet had to be grounded. Now, Ukrainian defense firm Rise Technologies has upgraded the drones with its Palych communications system, which allows the UAVs to withstand the advanced electronic warfare (EW) environment found on the frontlines in 2026. According to United24 Media, this new component allows drone operators to select the drone’s operating frequency band to avoid heavily jammed channels and maintain communications during flight. It also increases the range of the Puma to 31 miles (50 kilometers) from its basic range of 10 miles (16 kilometers).

Russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations to counter the countermeasures, like the use of fiber optic drones, which are essentially jam-proof, and the installation of a camera and magnetic compass on Russian drones to counter GPS jamming. Ukraine has also devised a "flying modem" relay system for its drones, allowing its forces to conduct strategic drone strikes even without the use of finicky Starlink connections. The indigenous communications system was also installed on other drones from DJI and Autel, as well as on some attack UAVs, giving Ukrainian drone operators an advantage on the battlefield.

The proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them. The U.S. has already deployed high-energy lasers to shoot down Mexican cartel drones crossing its southern border, while the Royal Navy is testing the DragonFire laser that can target UAVs traveling at up to 400 mph while only costing $13 per shot. Israel has also deployed its 100,000-watt Iron Beam system, while China has built a man-portable anti-drone laser system that weighs 55 pounds and can hit targets up to 1,600 feet away.

These laser systems are ideal for taking down a few drone units. But for drone swarm threats, microwave systems are a better solution, as they could take down multiple drones in a single shot. Some examples of this include the Leonidas AGV from the U.S. and Turkey’s Aselsan Ejderha, or “Dragon” in English, which uses high-power electromagnetic systems to overwhelm the sensitive electronics found inside most drones.

#10395. How Much Latency Does a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Add? Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

The bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

The first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:

On a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

Before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems.

KFC Spain has kicked off a new marketing campaign that leans on the recent digital-only Grand Theft Auto VI release. In 2026, gamers have become numb to digital-only releases, piles of early bugs, and multiple layers of DRM. However, as GTA 6 is such a highly anticipated release, folks are still entitled to moan about the physical Blu-ray-style case, which opens to reveal absolutely no physical media at all, just a vacant plastic hub and a redeemable online code. KFC Spain is putting things right, as best as it can, by giving away a free fried chicken disc to those bringing their empty game cases to select outlets in the country.

'The Replacement Disc' campaign is a pretty simple proposition. You can buy and enjoy your GTA 6 release now, but on December 19 and 20 from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM, take your empty game case down to KFC to get a free KFC disc. Branches where you can get this freebie food are located in major Spanish cities like Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Malaga, and Zaragoza.

The KFC disc will be formed from a piece of crunchy coated fried chicken, of course. While it surely will taste better than a platter of polycarbonate with a reflective metal alloy layer, it is only a substitute in spirit. We don't recommend you put greasy food directly in your game's case, even though it is basically useless. Definitely don't put your chicken disc anywhere near your console's optical media slot, if it has one.

GTA 6, released on November 19, is already a barnstorming success. The latest in this seminal series brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games said. That's about 5x the revenue of its predecessor. An incredible 32.5 million units were sold before release, and broke records across all platforms. So, it is canny for KFC to hitch its marketing wagon to this game, in such an unofficial but knowing social media-friendly way.

KFC has something of a track record of marketing off the back of tech and gaming culture. Its most famous tech adventure is probably the KFC Chicken Bucket Console. But more recently, last year, it teamed up with Asus to release some top-of-the-line burgers made from Wagyu beef with ROG branding.

#10390. Google homepage rolling out AI-focused redesign that includes your Gemini chats [Video]

The Google Search homepage is embracing Gemini in a big way, with a new sidebar redesign that puts your chat history just a click away.

Google’s AI ambitions have been anything but subtle in their integration with Search, but Gemini and Search have had some clear separations. But, with its latest update, Google is very much intertwining the two.

Confirmed by Google’s Robby Stein on Twitter/X, Google is now rolling out a desktop homepage revamp that gives Gemini near-top billing.

At first glance, you’ve got the typical blank canvas with a Google logo and Search bar at the center, but the new changes start with Gemini-powered shortcuts underneath for actions such as creating images, analyzing files, and “brainstorming” with Gemini.

These replace the existing “Google Search” button.

Beyond that, a new sidebar pulls your Gemini chat history and tasks into the Search homepage as well as including a “New chat” shortcut and everything else you’d find in the Gemini desktop app/site. The AI-heavy adjustment is very perhaps one of the biggest embraces of AI in Search since Google launched AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Stein explains this change is because users are coming to Search with questions that aren’t “one and done.”

People are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.

The new Google Search homepage is now rolling out globally, Stein says, though we’re not seeing it live just yet on our devices. Sound off in the comments if you’re seeing the new look and whether or not you like this functionality.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk’s Neuralink started clinical trials less than three years ago, and patients are seeing impressive results. The latest demonstration of this brain computer interface comes via a video on social media showing an unnamed medical trial participant playing GTA 6. According to the video, the team behind the implant mapped different i,agined movements to a PlayStation 5 controller, allowing the player to simulate controller actions using his thoughts. For example, thinking about tapping their ring finger activated the square button while imagining sliding their right hand forward pulled the nose of the airplane up. They also mentioned another control being bound to their foot, it’s unclear what action this allowed.

Playing GTA VI with a Neuralink https://t.co/ViFjXK9OSVNovember 20, 2026

The first Neuralink device was implanted in January 2024, with the patient able to move a mouse just by thinking. Once they’ve been able to master the basics of using a computer, like moving a mouse and using the keyboard, through the brain-computer interface (BCI), one of the next steps that some patients take is to play a game on their system. Just a couple of months after the first implant, we’ve already seen reports of people using Neuralink to play turn-based games like chess and Civilization VI. By August 2024, the second Neuralink recipient was reportedly playing Counter-Strike 2, with the patient calling the experience “insane.”

Today, we already have people playing complicated games like World of Warcraft and GTA VI using BCI implants. This is an achievement for Neuralink and a life-changing capability for patients who have lost mobility. The patient who streamed their GTA VI gameplay said that they’ve previously used a mouth stick, but it was miles away from the Neuralink chip they have in their head. “Before the … chip and surgery, I was using a mouth stick and an iPad. I was essentially like a bird just pecking at an iPad. There was (sic) like a few games I could play, but like obviously it made your jaw sore, it made everything sore,” the patient said. “So, then I get a chip, and I was like what does this let me do. Immediately, controlling a computer is like boom, ‘portal to the world,’ like you just immediately get your portal to the world back.”

Aside from giving people the ability to control computing devices with their mind, Neuralink is also working on a technology, called Blindsight, that will restore sight to blind people. Musk claims that it’s already “ready from an engineering standpoint,” and that the company is only waiting for regulatory approval before it can begin human testing.

#10388. Google’s 3D emoji has wild Android spec requirements: 10GB of free space, 6GB RAM

Google introduced 3D emoji on Pixel this year, and has just detailed the minimum specifications required to get them on your Android phone.

Update: Google replied on Reddit to “clear up some confusion” about the Help Center page. The listed storage and RAM requirements refer to the “automatic background download via Google Play services on eligible Android 17 devices that didn’t ship with the 3D font preinstalled.” The support article did not make that distinction.

Noto 3D emoji, with its high-resolution bitmap approach, uses less than 220 MB of storage versus the previous 2D vector font that comes in at around 3 MB.

During installation, Google Play services temporarily needs a bit of extra headroom to copy the file into place before immediately clearing its download cache.

Meanwhile, Google said RAM usage is “minimal & transient” as “Android doesn’t load the 3D emoji font file into RAM.” The support page listed 6 GB as a “cutoff to ensure lower-memory devices stay on the lightweight ~3 MB 2D vector font.”

Noto 3D emoji goes from vector-based 2D emoji to a high-resolution bitmap font. This results in “high-resolution designs” for emoji “with more texture and dimension to characters and icons.” Google has an FAQ section about why the new emoji might look low resolution:

Vector vs. bitmap rendering: Older Android emoji used 2D vector graphics, which scale infinitely to any size without losing resolution. The 3D emoji are bitmap graphics, which are pre-rendered pixel-based images. When these images are scaled up by an app or zoomed in, the pixels stretch, which can cause a softer or lower-resolution appearance.

The Google support article published this week lists the minimum specs your Android device must have to get 3D emoji:

The last two bullet points are rather surprising. In fact, Google even lists instructions for checking how much memory and storage your device has:

In terms of availability, Google says a supported device will “automatically download the 3D emoji when it’s on Wi-Fi and charging.”

At this time, there isn’t a way to force download the emoji.

Google announced 3D emoji in May, with the new design shipping on the Pixel 11 in August. It has since arrived on older Pixel devices.

In terms of OEM availability, Google explicitly says “Samsung devices use a proprietary emoji font and do not receive the 3D font update.” Additionally:

This is also true for third-party messaging apps, such as WhatsApp, who use their own emoji fonts rather than relying on your device’s system font.

#10386. Find Orphan Pages and Buried Content: Build an Internal Link Graph for Your Site

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will quickly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

If a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an important page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

The desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Important pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

A couple of examples of how a deep page is present:

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:

Wasted links are those internal links that do not do the job they're supposed to do. The different types of wasted links:

We have seen here how to look at our own website through the lens of a search engine. You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking issues; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

Based on the know-how accumulated while leading the development of the Galaxy series for a long time, he is expected to lead innovation in foldable phones, on-device AI, and wearables.

It’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto VI is now a real thing that we all can play. Thirteen years after GTA V, and eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar is back with its latest sprawling, extravagant open world. There’s a lot to experience — and a lot to talk about.

Perhaps the most impressive thing about GTA VI is how flexible it is, letting you mold the experience to your own play style. You can still be a maniacal criminal, but you can also focus on the new love story that includes an entire button dedicated to holding hands. Or you can spend the hours fishing or driving around listening to the radio. Maybe you just want to doomscroll through a fake version of Instagram. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me just ahead of launch, “It’s a risk. It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”

Now that the game is out and people are finding their own way through Leonida, it’s a great time to start talking about it. I’ve played through the entire main story — you can read my review right here — but I’m nowhere close to experiencing everything in the game. But I’m happy to answer any questions you have, though I’ll be careful around some of the big story spoilers. I’ll also be joined by senior reporter Jay Peters, who is still early in the game and can offer a different perspective. There’s a good chance some other Verge staff will stop by as well, since we’re basically all playing it.

So drop all of your questions, theories, and stray thoughts about GTA VI here. I’ll be checking in throughout the day to join the conversation in the comments.
