#10334. How to Build a Unified Lead Tracking Pipeline for Web Forms and Phone Calls

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report shows two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

This tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:

const params = new URL(url).searchParams;

"utm_source", "utm_medium", "utm_campaign",

return Object.fromEntries(keys.flatMap(key => {

The browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:

"occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",

The event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

"form.submitted", "call.started", "call.completed",

export function makeEvent(input, trusted) {

const ids = [trusted.tenantId, trusted.source,

if (ids.some(id => typeof id !== "string" ||

throw new TypeError("Invalid event identifiers");

throw new TypeError("Unsupported event type");

const time = Date.parse(input.occurredAt);

if (typeof input.occurredAt !== "string" ||

new Date(time).toISOString() !== input.occurredAt) {

throw new TypeError("Expected a canonical UTC timestamp");

attribution_ref: input.attributionRef ?? null,

Resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

For a form, issue a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a new one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

Authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

Here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id)

The ingestion function below accepts a pg pool and a normalized event. Install pg in your Node.js project, save the function as persist.mjs, and initialize the pool using your application's database configuration.

export async function persistEvent(pool, event) {

const key = [event.tenant_id, event.source, event.event_id];

const values = [...key, JSON.stringify(event)];

await client.query("BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED");

ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, source, event_id) DO NOTHING

WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND source = $2 AND event_id = $3

const error = new Error("Event ID reused with new data");

INSERT INTO crm_outbox (tenant_id, source, event_id)

return { inserted: inserted.rowCount === 1 };

PostgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

This depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a new event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

#10331. Clicks Communicator hits a supply chain snag, and it isn’t because of RAM

Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

The Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

Last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery update detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a new update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain issues caused by something other than RAM.

Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the company’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

The post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded issues have pushed production back, and users are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese New Year.

In an act of good faith, Clicks says it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

A mere 200 MHz chip with hyper-optimized software is enough to destroy all humans.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Readers with back pain probably recall the much-discussed 1996 chess challenge, wherein the world champion Gerry Kasparov faced off against IBM's Deep Blue chess-optimized computer. The nascent clanker lost the match with a 4-2 total, but still stunned the world by being the first piece of electric sand to win a single game against a grandmaster. Modern chess engines will utterly destroy any human, but Anthropic engineer Nicholas Carlini wondered if granting old hardware new bytes would give the machine a better chance. Spoiler: yes, indeed it would.

To understand the task, here's a quick primer on chess scoreboards. A player is rated worldwide with an Elo system (first devised for chess), wherein they lose or gain points in proportion to the difference to their opponent's rating — meaning that winning a match against Magnus Carlsen would net you a lot of points versus defeating me, who only learned about the en passant rule a handful of years ago.

At his prime, Kasparov ranked about 2800 points. Given that Deep Blue eventually barely won against him in a subsequent rematch, that is a good starting point for any. Contemporary chess engines like Stockfish have an estimated Elo of about 3,300, far higher than any human — guaranteeing it'll win most matches against a human.

Nicholas Carlini got hold of a 1995-era machine, packing a Pentium Pro CPU with all of its 200 MHz of clock speed, and 64 MB of RAM. For his first experiment, he grabbed Crafty, a 1996 chess engine, and measured how well it would do. It came in at 2,000 Elo with 1 second allotted, and 2,400 @ 10s. Running that software on a Ryzen 7 resulted in a 2,600 rating — good, but not enough.

Since Crafty's source code is available, he got Claude to mod it with modern features, and eventually reached a ceiling of 3,000 Elo @ 10s per move. That's quite an impressive feat already, especially considering that the lone Pentium Pro represented but a small fraction of the hardware that Deep Blue had. An Elo delta of +200 means this iteration would defeat Kasparov three out of every four games, while a +400 delta means a victory nine out of ten times.

Carlini then pulled out the big gun: Stockfish. He had to ask Claude to modify it to use only 32-bit arithmetic instead of 64-bit, and limit its workspace to the measly 64 MB of RAM, minus whatever the system harness took. Right off the bat, the figures were revealing: 2,500 @ 1s, and 3000 @ 10s.

The engineer performed a few optimization passes, and eventually got 2,850 @ 1s; 3,100 @ 10s; and almost 3,200 @ 30s — enough to put every human in their place, especially in a grandmaster tournament setting where there's no fixed time per move. You can play the bot using the link on the respective blog post. We'd wish you the best of luck, but there's no such concept in chess.

#10324. Securing FastAPI Applications: JWT Authentication and Rate Limiting with Redis

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

In this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:

Security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

Hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

To handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

Redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

Next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:

Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

We also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

The login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

Once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:

If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

To validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid users.

Next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

Building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

While this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

The lowest rungs of hell may be reserved for politicians, yes, but scalpers have a gated community somewhere in the same area code. The latest emotion-inducing story on this topic comes from Ontario, Canada, wherein a person from Oakville had an ad listing what appear to be over forty RTX 5090s for sale, priced at 9,500 CAD (over $6,600 USD) for the cheapest, and also having the gall to demand an extra 500 CAD (about $350 USD) for one with a sealed box.

The magnanimous magnate wanted to perform the transactions at his nearby police station, and claimed that "testing is available." Some Canadian police stations do open their lobbies for this purpose for added public safety. The scalper said in his ad that he had models from most every manufacturer, including Nvidia's Founders Edition and even Dell.

Should the statements by commenter "goudacheeseguy" be true, the person selling the card is their business partner. The cards purportedly came from their small neocloud outfit and are being sold as they eventually got their hands on Nvidia B300, B200, and Pro 6000 servers "with the money [they] made shorting AI funnily enough." It's possible they're telling the truth, as the presence of the Dell and Nvidia FE cards, plus the fact they're apparently mostly open-box units, would fit with that story.

Nevertheless, the response from commenters was swift and harsh. Some pointed out that the photograph depicting windows of a street-level basement, coupled with the fact that Oakville isn't that huge, could have a master geo-guesser like Rainbolt pinpointed where the scalper was.

In a similar vein, other people remarked on the danger of the seller being followed home for discussing a five-finger discount. His laissez-faire attitude infuriated some commenters, as he stated that "[he has] other models too probably missed some, too lazy to check which ones."

There's some irony in this story, however. It's safe to say that scalpers don't garner the same amount of love as puppies, and yet the 9,500 CAD he was asking for the cards is actually on par with or lower than commercial offerings. A commenter pointed out a Canadian Customs auction of an RTX 5090 that seemingly ended up selling for 8,300 CAD.

As of right now, an RTX 5090 at Memory Express will set you back around 10,000 CAD, and even the cheapest card at Newegg Canada is going for 9,300 CAD, though it's a pretty sweet combo deal (for these times), as you do get a motherboard, a case, and a power supply included in that price.

#10319. AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.

AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.

Research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which was, unbeknownst to users, copying secrets to a hidden file and committing them with the rest of the developer's code.

Among specific secrets leaked were "a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database," Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote in the post.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, "from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors," they wrote.

The issue stems from how coding assistants — Claude Code, in a specific case that the researchers examined — carry out certain commands. "Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file," the researchers explained.

The tool will ask the user before running the command and, if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," then "it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder," according to the report.

"Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code," the researchers explained.

The fact that a routine development task creates a security exposure is dangerous for organizations, especially because these AI coding tools are supposed to be helpful, not harmful, notes Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing for database security firm Liquibase.

“A developer approves a command to save time, the AI agent retains credentials as part of that approval, and those credentials can eventually end up in a public repository," he observes via email. "Nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible."

In the case of Claude Code, Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, finding that 1,122 files contained real secrets. The researchers identified 1,379 distinct secrets in those files alone, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

Claude Code is not being overtly careless; it does try to protect files when it creates its .claude/settings.local.json file inside a Git repository, the researchers noted. The tool does this by adding the file to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore the file on that particular developer's machine. This prevents it from being included in routine commits.

However, the protection is not built into the development project itself, and the "ignore" rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, the researchers noted. "The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it," they wrote.

Moreover, Claude Code itself was sometimes responsible for committing the exposed files. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file.

The action that exposes these secrets while using Claude Code appears to be a "dead zone" of sorts for developers using AI coding assistants, so they likely have no idea that they've just exposed a secret, observes Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

"A 'don't ask again' prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file, and many developers clicking it likely don't know that file exists," he says. "Once it lands in a repository, it sits in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through."

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing the findings. After their publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, said in public comments that although Claude Code historically has not done secrets scrubbing, the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure described by Apiiro, according to Apiiro's report.

Those approaches may be to make sure auto mode catches the exposure, or to build in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas that Anthropic will prototype "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping something with its next version of Claude Code, Cherny said.

Indeed, the leakage exposes how Claude Code's protection relies heavily on a developer-specific Git setting rather than a safeguard built into the project or the AI coding tool itself, exposing a gap that can turn an ordinary command approval into a persistent credential leak.

To avoid this, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held, and open all fields and delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Meanwhile, security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repos, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

"As AI agents become more involved in software development, organizations need to recognize that source code isn't the only thing they need to secure," McCurdy observes. "Agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information, and traditional security checks may not catch everything."

The stock BIOS only had room for two 32GB cards, and custom fan ducts handle the heat.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A homelabber has built a local AI system out of four used 32GB Nvidia V100s and a refurbished Lenovo M720q Tiny mini PC. Ok_Kaleidoscope9103’s construction, detailed on Reddit, relies on the GPUs going over four OCuLink cables from a PCIe switch card, with a solder bridge on the riser and coreboot getting past a BIOS that only booted two cards. The quiet-running build has the full 128GB of VRAM and can hit about 285 tokens per second in total running Qwen3.8-27B across its four cards.

The user, who gives his name as Michael, details his “home AI box” in a YouTube video billed as a “full build guide.” The Australian builder describes the setup as “four docks, four datacentre cards, one little PC” in a “noise optimised build.”

The hardware for this particular build is based on a Lenovo M720q Tiny desktop, which has an i5-9400T CPU with 64GB of DDR4. With a matching Lenovo 01AJ940 riser and a CEACENT CNOL4PE08 PCIe switch card — this has a 24-lane PEX8724 switch on board for an x8 link in and four x4 OCuLink ports out — each GPU card can run at PCIe Gen3 x4. OCuLink is an external PCIe cable connector often used with external GPUs (eGPU).

On the software and firmware end, the Tiny had some roadblocks that had to be overcome. It “only powers its riser slot when the card pulls the presence pin,” which the switch card doesn’t, so a solder bridge was needed on the back of the riser. Then, “Lenovo’s BIOS only leaves a 128 GB window for 64-bit devices,” and each 32GB V100 needs 64GB, which limits the stock firmware to just two cards; a third “hangs at POST.”

His workaround used coreboot 26.09 built for the board with an EDK2 payload and a config setting that allows above-4G allocation. This expands the window to about 486GB and, with three patches, more features were enabled: the riser slot is always on, there is a Wake-on-LAN override, and merged memory type range registers (MTRRs). Flashing it needed a CH341A programmer and SOIC8 clip for the BIOS chip.

He then added four AOOSTAR AG01 eGPU docks, each with a built-in 800 W PSU, and assigned one V100 to each dock. Each dock’s PSU feeds its V100 through a dual PCIe 8-pin to CPU/EPS 8-pin adapter, because the card takes a CPU 8-pin. The Tesla V100s are otherwise passively cooled and rely on chassis or other external airflow.

Then there’s the matter of cooling without ear-bleeding. The V100s each get a 3D-printed 140 mm funnel — designed with the help of AI — with a Noctua NF-A14 iPPC-3000 fan, with all four driven on an ARCTIC 10-port USB fan controller. A separate ARCTIC P12 Silent is mounted in a Dremel-drilled hole in the Tiny’s lid to cool the switch card, as that does run hot. He measured the end result at about 62 dB at a distance of one meter.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

A script tracks the hottest card, stopping work at 83°C and powering the system off at 87°C. To keep temperatures in check, each card is also power-capped to 200 W, or 800 W total. A recent, separate dual-GPU build we detailed needs dual 12W fans to keep the Optane and system memory cool.

With this 4-card setup, 44.7 TFLOPS is doable with FP32 with a 71°C peak; this compares to Nvidia’s rating of 14 TFLOPS for each 250 W card. A single RTX 5090 is rated at 104.8 TFLOPS at 575 W, nearly double the 56 TFLOPS of four V100s. Qwen3.8-27B Q6 can chat at about 40 tokens per second with one card and about 285 per second with all four, each card running its own copy and handling four requests at once. A larger model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-125B-A6B IQ4_XS, does about 43 tokens per second on chat over all four, or about 116 with eight requests.

The builder says that this cost him “~A$6.5k all-in,” a figure that includes local taxes; he puts it closer to $3,500 in U.S. dollars. Check the table for the cost breakdown. As noted in our coverage of other V100 builds, the cost of some of this hardware — SXM2 V100s, in particular — has climbed significantly this year; he says his PCIe cards “jumped in price” in recent months.

Although he calls using the full 128GB a “party trick,” he actually does use the build with Qwen3.8-27B, running separately on each card, to mine stock-announcement data dating back to the early 1990s for his business, which needs to read “millions of documents.” The build has been stable, running “pretty much 24/7 for a few weeks,” and with this setup he expects the system to pay itself back in about three months.

Some commenters wonder why he didn’t take the route of a fellow Redditor, a lawyer, who experimented with 32GB V100s as SXM2 modules on NVLink boards. His answer: noise, and that “the PCIe cards at the time were cheaper.” He also compares his four V100s to an RTX 5090, and says they have 4x the VRAM and about 2x the total memory bandwidth at “about half the price” of a 5090 in Australia. Next up is benchmarking SFNX and Infer-V100 to see how it compares to his llama.cpp setup.cpp setup, and possibly adding a second set of four V100s.

#10317. Is the Galaxy S26 Ultra still a good buy at the end of 2026?

Yes, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra remains a good buy in late 2026 if you want a large-screen Android phone with versatile cameras, an integrated S Pen, and long-term software support.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra has aged very well, benefiting from Samsung’s mature hardware and software, along with a host of other quality-of-life improvements gained from its recent update to One UI 9 running Android 17.

We’re going to take a deeper dive at what the S26 Ultra is, and how it compares to its cheaper siblings, in a quest to figure out whether it’s still worth your time and money this holiday season.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is the highest-end model in Samsung’s 2026 Galaxy S26 lineup. Released back on March 11, it pairs a 6.9-inch display with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor, a built-in S Pen, and a four-camera system led by a 200MP main sensor.

It’s a powerful device, built for photography enthusiasts and professionals who want to get the most out of their phones while on the go. Its large screen size belies a relatively compact, portable device that’s a pleasure to do work on, from writing emails to taking photos to taking meeting notes using the S Pen.

We also found dependable everyday endurance from the 5,000mAh battery, and now that the phone supports 60-watt wired charging, quick top-ups become more useful. Samsung also promises seven generations of OS upgrades and seven years of security updates from launch, an important consideration if you plan to keep your next phone for several years.

At launch, US pricing started at $899.99 for the Galaxy S26, $1,099.99 for the Galaxy S26+, and $1,299.99 for the Galaxy S26 Ultra, each with 256GB of storage. But those prices have dropped over the past few months, and you may be able to get them for less. We’ve seen the S26 Ultra, for example, as low as $999.99 during Prime Day.

Having different lenses gives you more options for portraits, travel photos, and subjects you can’t easily walk closer to.

The regular Galaxy S26 is the more natural choice if you prioritize a smaller phone and a lower purchase price. The Galaxy S26+ makes sense if you want a large-screen Galaxy without paying for Ultra-specific features.

The biggest improvement since launch is the move from Android 16-based One UI 8.5 to Android 17-based One UI 9.

One UI 9 offers several practical additions. Now Nudge suggestions extend beyond the keyboard into conversation notifications and a floating button. The quick panel offers more customization, and Samsung DeX gains easier movement between desktops and desktop previews in Recents.

Samsung has also made Smart Switch even better, which allows you to quickly and easily port over your apps, data, and media from another device.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s features are most useful when they solve problems or make everyday moments feel joyful and seamless. Here are five examples:

If you’re coming from a Galaxy S22 or S23 series phone, there are so many upgrades, small and large, that are awaiting you with the S26 Ultra.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra and Samsung’s other products are on sale during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

#10315. How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Cloud Range's free 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment helps organizations identify gaps in operational technology (OT) incident response.

Cloud Range introduces a 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment to help organizations identify gaps in preparedness for cyberattacks affecting operational technology.

The assessment covers seven critical areas, from OT asset visibility and IT/OT coordination to incident detection, response, recovery, and readiness validation.

Recent OT cybersecurity research reinforces the importance of preparing IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to investigate and respond to attacks that can disrupt physical operations.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Cyberattacks affecting operational technology (OT) can disrupt production, equipment, and essential services, resulting in consequences that extend beyond disruptions to traditional IT systems. To help organizations evaluate their preparedness, Cloud Range today introduced the Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment, a free, 28-question resource designed to identify potential gaps in OT incident response preparedness.

Related:Industrial Serial Gateways Broadcast That They're Insecure

The assessment provides a practical starting point for IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to evaluate how well they understand their environments, coordinate responsibilities, and prepare to detect, investigate, respond to, and recover from cyber incidents affecting industrial operations.

“Organizations can have incident response plans, security tools, and experienced teams in place without knowing how effectively those capabilities will work together when an attack affects operations,” said Debbie Gordon, CEO of Cloud Range. “The first step is understanding where teams are prepared, where they may be relying on assumptions, and where further validation is needed. The stakes are different in OT because decisions made during a cyber incident can have direct operational consequences.”

Recent research illustrates the scale of cyber threats facing industrial organizations. The Dragos 2026 OT Cybersecurity Year in Review reports that approximately 3,300 industrial organizations were affected by ransomware in 2025.

Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 State of Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Report found that 59% of surveyed critical infrastructure organizations experienced a significant security breach in the past year. The research also found that 74% had not fully integrated IT and OT security operations, highlighting the importance of coordinated incident response.

The report also identifies operational consequences of cybersecurity incidents, including safety concerns, unplanned downtime, production disruptions, and financial losses.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Together, these findings underscore a central challenge for organizations operating OT and industrial control systems (ICS): preventing attacks is important, but so is understanding whether teams can recognize, investigate, and respond quickly and effectively when incidents occur.

An attack does not have to originate within an OT network to affect industrial operations. Compromises involving enterprise IT systems, third-party access, supply chains, or interconnected infrastructure can create consequences for production environments and critical services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment examines seven areas that influence an organization's ability to prepare for and respond to cyberattacks affecting OT environments:

Know Your Environment: Understand critical OT assets, systems, dependencies, and connections between IT and OT environments.

Know Your Threats and Stakes: Recognize relevant cyber threats and their potential impact on operations, equipment, and safety.

Bridge IT and OT: Establish shared responsibilities, communication, and decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Detect and Investigate: Identify suspicious activity, investigate threats, and determine their potential operational consequences.

Respond Without Making It Worse: Make coordinated incident response decisions that account for production continuity, equipment, and safety.

Recover and Maintain Resilience: Understand recovery priorities, system dependencies, and procedures for restoring critical operations.

Prove Readiness Before It Matters: Validate response capabilities through realistic cyberattack simulations and measurable performance.

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Each area includes three questions, with responses of Ready, Developing, or Unsure.

Rather than assigning a numerical score, the assessment helps organizations identify gaps, uncertainties, and areas requiring further attention. IT, security, OT, and engineering teams can complete it independently and compare their responses to uncover differences in understanding, unclear responsibilities, or differing assumptions about preparedness.

Why OT Incident Response Preparedness Requires Cross-Functional Coordination

OT environments present distinct incident response challenges because cyber decisions can affect physical equipment, industrial processes, production availability, and potentially safety.

Actions that may be appropriate in an enterprise IT environment, such as isolating a system or shutting down a device, can require additional operational evaluation when industrial systems are involved.

Effective OT incident response therefore depends on coordination among teams with different responsibilities and expertise.

IT and security personnel may focus on identifying malicious activity, containing threats, and investigating compromised systems. OT and engineering personnel understand process dependencies, equipment limitations, and the operational consequences of response decisions.

Both perspectives are essential. The integration gap identified in the Palo Alto Networks research reinforces the importance of shared understanding, clear responsibilities, and coordinated decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Understanding how to assess OT cyber readiness across these functions helps organizations identify where their procedures, communication, and decision-making may require further attention.

The assessment is intended to support those conversations before an actual incident demands coordinated action.

An assessment can help organizations identify preparedness gaps, but it cannot establish how effectively teams will perform during a real cyber incident.

That requires opportunities to investigate attacks, make decisions, coordinate across functions, and evaluate the results in realistic environments.

Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen critical infrastructure cyber readiness, realistic cloud-based OT/ICS, IT, cloud, and hybrid environments where teams can investigate cyber threats, coordinate incident response, and measure performance. Its critical infrastructure cybersecurity and readiness programs help organizations prepare for attacks that may disrupt industrial processes, equipment, and essential services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Range supports flat and Purdue-model industrial network architectures, allowing teams to investigate how connectivity, segmentation, and system dependencies influence attack progression and response. Hardware-in-the-loop capabilities can also connect physical OT laboratory equipment to the cyber range for cyber-physical security validation.

Through OT cyberattack simulations and adversary emulation, teams can investigate ransomware, supply-chain compromise, credential theft, lateral movement, and threats affecting industrial systems.

Performance metrics highlight how teams improve in detecting threats, investigating activity, coordinating decisions, and improving incident response over time.

Across Cloud Range customer engagements, measured improvements have included reductions of up to 66% in mean time to detect and improvements of up to 30% in overall incident response time. These results reflect broader cyber readiness programs and are not specific to OT environments.

As IT and OT environments become more interconnected, organizations face growing pressure to understand both their cybersecurity exposure and their ability to respond to incidents with operational consequences.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment provides a structured way to evaluate preparedness across seven critical areas. Organizations can use the findings to prioritize improvements and identify where realistic attack-based validation can provide stronger evidence of readiness.

The objective is not simply to have an incident response plan. It is to build confidence that the people, processes, and technologies involved can work together when an attack affects operations.

Cloud Range is the leader in Cyber Readiness and Validation, helping organizations continuously measure and improve how people, processes, and AI perform under real-world attack conditions. As the creator of the industry's first full-service, cloud-based cyber range, Cloud Range provides realistic IT, OT/ICS, and cloud environments where organizations can safely train, test, validate, measure, and benchmark cyber readiness across people, processes, and AI agents.

Used by enterprise organizations, government agencies, higher education institutions, critical infrastructure organizations, and managed security service providers (MSSPs), Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen cyber readiness through live-fire cyberattack simulations, objective performance measurement, expert guidance, continuous readiness programs, and AI validation.

Cloud Range has received multiple industry awards recognizing innovation and leadership in cyber readiness, cyber defense, and cybersecurity excellence and has been recognized by leading analyst and research organizations for its contributions to cyber readiness, cyber ranges, AI validation, and modern security operations. Google’s Fitbit Air is one of my favorite products of 2026 and my preferred workout companion, but not being able to see a workout while you’re in the middle of it has been a huge complaint of mine, and the latest Google Health update is fixing that.

#10313. How AI Image-to-Image and Image-to-Video Tools Work, and How to Build a Reliable Workflow

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Creating polished visual content used to require professional equipment, editing skills and hours of manual work. Generative AI has changed that for photographers, designers, marketers and developers who build creative tools, but the results depend heavily on understanding what these systems actually do. Two techniques sit at the center of most workflows: image-to-image generation, which transforms an existing picture, and image-to-video generation, which adds motion to a still.

This article explains how both techniques work, which settings control the outcome, how several kinds of tools differ, and how to assemble a workflow with review steps, including a short code example you can run yourself. It also covers rights, authenticity and the limits of the technology. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you plan a production.

Image-to-image resembles text-to-image, but it starts from your picture instead of pure noise. According to the Hugging Face Diffusers image-to-image guide, the initial image is encoded into latent space and noise is added to it. The model then uses the prompt and the noisy latent to predict and remove that noise, and a decoder converts the result back into an image.

A single setting, usually called strength or creativity, decides how much of the original remains. In Diffusers, a higher strength gives the model more freedom, and a value of 1.0 means the starting image is largely ignored. Strength is linked to the number of denoising steps: with 50 inference steps and a strength of 0.8, the pipeline adds noise for 40 steps and then denoises for 40.

The ranges above are rules of thumb, not guarantees. Models and tools respond differently, so test on your own images. The script below, adapted from the Diffusers documentation, sweeps four strength values on one source image so you can compare them side by side.

Running this requires a compatible GPU setup and model downloads, and the checkpoint name and defaults can change between library versions, so check the current documentation.

Plain image-to-image can drift from the layout you wanted. Research such as ControlNet adds spatial control to pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, with conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation and human pose. In practice, this is why many tools offer reference images, sketches, masks and pose guides on top of a prompt: they supply structure that a text prompt cannot describe precisely.

The key advantage is speed of iteration. The main limits are consistency between variations, small details such as hands and text, and the gap between a convincing concept and a usable final asset.

The right tool depends on what you need to control and where the output will be used. The table summarizes what each vendor’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

OpenArt’s own page describes an AI image to image generator that accepts JPEG, PNG, WEBP or HEIC files, offers a creativity slider and an optional reference image, and lets you switch between several models. Its FAQ advises uploading only images you own or have rights to use. Adobe’s Firefly page describes generative editing and video tools and states that outputs include Content Credentials, while saying its own models were trained on licensed and public-domain content. These are vendor statements, so read the current terms for the plan you use.

Image-to-video uses a still as the starting point for an animated scene. Most current systems extend diffusion models across time, so that a whole sequence of frames is denoised together. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequence is that the first frame strongly shapes what follows, so a clean composition and a clear subject make better clips.

For example, a still of a person walking through a rainy city can be animated with falling rain, reflections and a slow camera move. The motion instruction should describe one clear action and one camera movement rather than a long list.

Kling’s main site announces Kling 4.0 and describes stable dynamic motion with an audio-visual experience, with image-to-video features and an API platform listed. OpenArt’s Kling 4.0 page describes how the model is offered on that platform. According to that page, videos run from 3 to 30 seconds at 720p to 1080p, you can use up to 10 keyframes and up to 15 references, and you can save a character for reuse. The page does not state pricing or generation quotas for the model. Capabilities depend on the platform that provides access and on the settings available there, so check supported inputs, output limits and cost before planning a production.

Generated motion needs checking. Warped limbs, drifting faces, flickering textures and unwanted text are common. A quick review script samples frames and reports basic file properties:

Consider a small business preparing a campaign for a new skincare product. The same steps apply to any visual project.

This process reduces the effort of exploring concepts and makes it easier to test several versions of an advertisement before choosing a direction. It does not remove the need for human review.

They can be, with different priorities. Photographers can explore creative treatments, mood boards and alternative backgrounds without replacing traditional photography. Marketers can develop campaign concepts, create variations of social graphics and test promotional videos. In both cases the value comes from supporting a clear creative objective rather than adopting a tool because it is new.

A technique that transforms an existing image using a prompt, by adding noise to the image and then regenerating it under guidance. A strength or creativity setting controls how much of the original is kept.

Use a lower strength, a reference image or a structure condition such as edges or depth where the tool supports it.

Yes. Image-to-video tools animate a still from a motion description, though complex motion can introduce inconsistencies, so review every clip.

No. Several vendors and platforms offer video generation. Compare supported inputs, length, resolution, cost and licensing against your needs.

It depends on the tool, the plan and the rights you hold in the inputs. Read the current terms and keep records of your sources.

Image-to-image and image-to-video tools give creators a faster way to explore ideas, but they work best when you understand their controls. Strength settings decide how much of the original survives, conditioning methods preserve structure, and the starting frame shapes video. Compare hosted platforms, vendor apps and open-source libraries against your needs, build review and provenance into the workflow, and treat the output as a draft that a person checks before it ships.

This weird "finger-worn gaming mouse" has reached $43,000 in its Kickstarter campaign.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Borslon wearable gaming mouse takes the concept of a gaming mouse to the extreme by making your finger the aiming device. The Kickstarter has already reached over $43,000 with more than 430 backers, beating its $5,000 goal — but is it truly innovative, or just a gimmick?

The Borslon mouse, sharing a product and brand name, is a wired, “finger-worn gaming mouse,” as the brand describes it. It has all the spec numbers you’d expect from a good gaming mouse: a PAW3395 sensor, an 8,000 Hz polling rate, 0.125 ms response time, programmable buttons, and weighs 36g. However, the specs are often only the base level for performance; how it performs in the real world could be a very different story.

This product targets FPS gamers, and in the FPS gaming niche, there is an even smaller niche — aimers. These aiming communities focus purely on the mechanical skill of precisely landing shots on targets, experimenting with techniques and devices to improve their aim. The community explores various aiming devices like tiny fingertip mice and even drawing tablets, with some brands directly marketing their mice in aiming Reddit groups.

The Borslon mouse isn’t the first extreme fingertip mouse; indie mice like the Precision Gaming Gear Titan-Ø and Titan-1 with their 3D-printed titanium construction and ruby joints launched years ago and sold out extremely quickly due to their popularity in the aiming niche.

There is reason to be skeptical of the Borslon mouse, as the videos alone don’t show even remotely impressive aiming examples, only playing against bots in Counter-Strike 2 with the player showing sub-par aim, while the creator of the Titan series mice showed decent actual gameplay in Quake Champions and is active in the aiming community.

Conventionally, many Counter-Strike, Apex Legends, and Valorant players use the scroll wheel for jumping or bunny-hopping (or tap strafing in Apex Legends, a high-level movement mechanic), and most players use their index or middle finger to scroll. However, the Borslon places the mouse wheel at the thumb, including the five programmable buttons, leaving plenty of responsibility to the appendage. From the Kickstart promotional material, it doesn’t look like the index finger or the middle finger have any buttons to press — which means the thumb is responsible for your usual inputs like aiming down sights (ADS), firing, and jumping; actions that usually happen simultaneously or in quick succession.

Borslon plans to ship out by February of 2027, with mass production planned for December, leaving little to no time to drastically change the design of the product.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

There is also an unusual disconnect between the mouse and its supposedly intended market, as I have not found any discussions about the Borslon mouse in any of the top aiming circles, nor is there any mention of it in the Voltaic Discord, a popular aiming community with over 200,000 members.

Upon further research, the Borslon brand is made by Shenzhen Komodo Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., with the Borslon website fully in Chinese, but neither the website nor the Kickstarter links to the other. A machine translation of the Borslon website of the company timeline says it released its first product in November 2025, while the Kickstarter says the concept initiation was in March 2026. The misalignments, combined with the heavy use of AI lifestyle images, don’t spark confidence in the project. If this is indeed real, it could potentially be a genuinely innovative mouse if the brand talked to the intended market and made proper changes.

Our customary crowdfunder disclaimer applies. Remember that crowdfunding a project is not a guarantee of receiving a finished product. Backing a crowdfunded project is akin to an investment; you believe in the project and want it to succeed. You are not purchasing a retail product.

#10310. Best Buy brings back 4K Blu-ray discs with an expanding collection, in-store availability [U]

It’s been nearly three years since Best Buy decided to ditch selling physical copies of movies, stripping its inventory from both its brick-and-mortar stores and its online catalog. But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game.

As spotted by TheHDRoom on Twitter and on the 4K Blu-ray subreddit, Best Buy is now selling 14 different 4K Blu-rays on its website, marking another step in the brand’s slow return to selling physical media. These films include:

Technically, Blu-ray returned to Best Buy’s online storefront in August of 2025, when it opened a third-party marketplace similar to Amazon or Walmart. These titles, however, are shipped and sold by Best Buy. Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which launched in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. It shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise that The Odyssey is getting some special treatment; in addition to its status as a box office juggernaut, Nolan’s previous movie, Oppenheimer, initially sold out of physical copies in its first week of release in 2023.

Outside of these 14 titles, additional Blu-rays continue to be sold through Best Buy’s third-party marketplace.

Update, 11/20: Best Buy confirmed to The HD Room on Twitter that The Odyssey is just the first 4K Blu-ray to return to physical locations, as it plans to continue adding “some” Blu-rays back to its stores.

The Odyssey may/will be joined by other 4K UHD titles at Best Buy in the future: "The Odyssey inspired a homecoming of our own – some physical media is returning to Best Buy. Sometimes what’s old does become new (again). And we're still feeling nostalgic, so stay tuned." pic.twitter.com/wz9xhcdo4G

#10308. Nintendo Switch 2-ready smart glasses from Viture are at their lowest price ever (up to $160 off)

Viture’s smart display glasses offer official Switch 2 compatibility with the Mobile Dock Mini, and these Black Friday deals even come with free bonus controllers and other accessories.

One of the most annoying things about playing Ocarina of Time right now is that everyone in my home is at a different point in their save file. This makes it tough to be in the same room with others and not spoil something for them, but plugging in a pair of Viture glasses makes this much easier since no one else can see the screen inside the glasses I’m wearing.

You can get your own pair of Viture glasses with the Switch 2 Mobile Dock Mini for as low as $375. This pack comes with Viture Pro 2 glasses, which sport a pair of 120Hz micro-OLED displays with 1,600-nit peak brightness and built-in myopia adjustment diopters. They also weigh just 63g, making them comfortable for long gaming sessions.

The Mobile Dock Mini (on sale for $99 on its own) in the pack comes with a magnetic mount that attaches to the back of the Switch 2. This Dock lets you plug your Viture glasses in and also charges the Switch 2, thanks to the built-in 10,000mAh battery. That delivers more than double the Switch 2’s battery life, so you can clear several temples in Ocarina before even thinking of stopping to charge.

Most of Viture’s glasses are on sale and have extra free gifts, which you can see in the image above. This includes the company’s high-end Viture Beast model, which is on sale for $489 ($60 off). That’s the lowest price ever for the glasses.

Viture Beast upgrades the experience with a wider field of view (58 degrees), native 3DoF spatial tracking, and 9-level electrochromic lens dimming. Native spatial tracking means that you can pin the virtual monitor in space and move around as if it were a TV mounted on a wall. Beast doesn’t have diopters, so you’ll need to order prescription lenses if you need myopia adjustment.

The biggest discount of all is on Viture Luma Pro, which is down to $339 ($160 off). Luma Pro is Viture’s “Goldilocks” pair with excellent image quality and RGB lighting along the frames for some extra style, and even includes myopia adjustment diopters. Pair any of these Viture glasses with the Mobile Dock Mini for Switch 2 compatibility, making them the only pair of smart glasses with official Switch 2 support.

Lastly is Viture Luma Ultra, down to $449 ($150 off). Luma Ultra sports the best image quality of all Viture glasses and includes myopia-adjusting diopters. These are the only pair that support 6DoF tracking when using the Viture Spacewalker app thanks to the cameras on the front, but there’s no native 3DoF support like Beast has, so this functionality is limited to content you view through the app.
